strengths: Comprehensive and systematic experimental evaluation across multiple VLM families (Owen3-VL, Molmo2), benchmarks (V*, HRBench), and resolutions with consistent improvements demonstrated
Clear practical value: achieves meaningful efficiency gains (20-30% token reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy across different computational budgets
Well-motivated approach grounded in neuroscience with intuitive two-stage pipeline that cleanly separates perception and reasoning concerns
Solid technical execution with thorough ablations (Tables 2-3, Appendices) investigating design choices like WBF fusion, consistency constraints, and fine-tuning strategies
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters (Table 4), training procedures, prompts (Appendix A.4), and qualitative analysis (Figures 6-9) enable verification and replication
Consistently outperforms 'thinking with images' baseline across models, with substantial improvements in some settings (Owen3-VL 4B: 40.9% → 51.0% on V* 256px)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: decouples perception and reasoning using known techniques (IRD/bounding box detection, WBF fusion). The contribution is primarily an incremental application of existing ideas to VLM test-time scaling rather than fundamental innovation

Mechanistic understanding unclear: lacks deep analysis of why decoupling perception improves scaling. Claims about 'asymmetric compute allocation' enabling better scaling need stronger theoretical or empirical justification beyond empirical results

Generalization concerns: approach is specialized to perception-centric VQA tasks with object localization. Applicability to reasoning-heavy tasks, open-ended visual understanding, and tasks where visual search is inappropriate remains unclear

Annotation overhead and data quality issues: requires synthetic data generation with manual annotation (23,000 samples). Molmo2-4B underperformance attributed to 'weak supervision' raises questions about scalability and generalizability of the synthetic data approach

Experimental design fairness: 'Thinking with images' baseline comparisons use OOD resolution settings where baseline wasn't designed; SPARC uses additional synthetic fine-tuning data not available to baselines. Some baseline results appear surprisingly low, suggesting possible implementation discrepancies

Incomplete computational characterization: while token counts provided, wall-clock inference latency, memory consumption, and crop processing overhead are not analyzed. Efficiency-accuracy trade-off depends heavily on crop count but this relationship insufficiently explored

Narrow evaluation scope: benchmarks limited primarily to high-resolution VQA perception tasks (V*, remote sensing). No evaluation on diverse downstream tasks (instruction following, dense captioning, visual reasoning), limiting claims about general VLM scaling

Modest improvements in many settings: while consistent, many improvements are 1-3% accuracy points. Some gains may be attributable to fine-tuning benefits rather than architectural separation of perception and reasoning

Limited failure mode analysis: qualitative examples (Figures 6-9) provided but systematic analysis of when IRD selects wrong regions, why performance degrades with excessive crop expansion (Figure 5), and failure rate statistics are absent

Methodological specificity and added complexity: approach tightly coupled to VQA/localization task formulation. Weighted Box Fusion algorithm adds complexity not fully justified. Requirement for context engineering and specific prompting (Appendix A.4) suggests some fragility

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation within scope with multiple model families (Qwen3-VL, Molmo2) and detailed ablations (Tables 1-3)
Clear methodology and well-articulated two-stage architecture with helpful visual explanations (Figure 1)
Practical engineering contribution showing genuine efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs across different input resolutions
Detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameters (Table 4), training procedures, and prompt specifications (Appendix A.4)
Systematic analysis across multiple settings with expanded results tables (Tables 7-9) demonstrating consistency
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is a straightforward two-stage pipeline combining standard techniques (object detection, spatial reasoning, LoRA finetuning) without fundamental methodological innovation
Narrow evaluation scope restricted to single V* benchmark; lacks evaluation on established VLM benchmarks (MMBench, MMVP) limiting generalizability claims
Insufficient statistical rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars despite sometimes marginal improvements (e.g., 51.0 vs 48.7 in Table 1)
Conceptual issues: claimed 'decoupling of perception and reasoning' is merely a sequential two-stage pipeline; asymmetric compute allocation principle is asserted without rigorous justification
Unfair baseline comparisons: 'thinking with images' baselines use different training procedures and hyperparameters, making it difficult to isolate SPARC's contribution
Limited generalization analysis: unclear whether approach benefits visual reasoning tasks beyond image crop identification or other VLM applications; insufficient ablations on key design choices
Shallow failure analysis with only 4 qualitative examples (Figures 6-9); minimal investigation of when/why method works or systematic analysis of failure modes
Missing comparisons with alternative efficient VLM approaches (dynamic resolution, token pruning, attention mechanisms) and lack of convergence/data efficiency analysis

strengths: Well-motivated neuroscience-inspired decomposition of VLM inference into perception (IRD) and reasoning stages, grounded in visual cortex architecture
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model families (Owen3-VL, Molmo2-4B/8B), resolutions (256, 512, Full), and computational budgets with systematic ablations
Significant practical efficiency gains demonstrated: 200× token budget reduction while improving accuracy by 6.7% on Owen3-VL-4B, with consistent improvements across benchmarks
Rigorous investigation of resolution compensation phenomenon with careful empirical validation of crop overlap ratios and their effects
Solid generalization study showing benefits extend across different model architectures and sizes, with explicit analysis of resolution-constrained variants
Detailed experimental documentation including hyperparameters (Table 4), prompts (A.4), and extensive ablation tables (Tables 7-9) supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation of core framework with excellent motivating figures and concrete qualitative examples (Figures 6-9) demonstrating SPARC's advantages over baselines
weaknesses: Implicit Relevance Detection (IRD) procedure lacks formal mathematical specification; presented heuristically without clear definition of how 'optimal' crops are selected at test time
Limited scope of evaluation primarily to VQA tasks (V*, HRBench); unclear if efficiency and accuracy benefits generalize to other VLM applications like captioning, dense prediction, or dialogue
Computational overhead of multiple crop generation and Weighted Box Fusion aggregation not fully accounted; claimed efficiency gains may be offset by increased test-time inference steps

Individual technical components (Chain-of-Thought, Self-Consistency, LoRA, visual grounding) are well-established; main contribution is engineering combination rather than introducing novel techniques
Reproducibility issues with Owen3-VL family mentioned but not analyzed or resolved, creating uncertainty about reliability of comparisons on primary benchmark
Modest absolute improvements on some models (e.g., Molmo2-4B shows smaller gains than Owen3-VL-4B); practical complexity of tuning crop sizes and overlap ratios may limit adoption
Limited failure mode analysis; no systematic categorization of question types or image characteristics where SPARC underperforms relative to baselines

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across multiple models, resolutions, and benchmarks with consistent improvements
Clear neuroscience-motivated architecture with intuitive design clearly communicated through effective visualizations
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating component contribution including WBF analysis, consistency strategies, and resolution ablations
Practical efficiency gains demonstrated - achieves strong performance at lower resolutions enabling actual computational savings
Well-documented reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters (Table 9), prompts (Appendix A.3), and implementation details
Addresses real practical challenges in VLM deployment regarding test-time scaling and context window management
Consistent performance gains across diverse model families (Qwen3-VL, Molmo2) and benchmarks (V*, HRBench, MME, GQA)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - core contribution is straightforward two-stage pipeline combining well-established techniques (bounding boxes, cropping, LoRA) rather than introducing new methods

Strong dependence on Implicit Relevance Detection (IRD) accuracy with limited failure mode analysis - stage 2 cannot recover from stage 1 errors, and approach cannot handle global scene understanding tasks

Incomplete computational cost analysis - actual end-to-end latency improvements not fully characterized, real-world deployment overhead underexplored, and TTFT/E2E metrics vary significantly across datasets
Evaluation scope limitations - primarily focuses on perception-QA tasks; reasoning-heavy tasks relegated to appendix; document OCR and chart reading scenarios not thoroughly evaluated
Weak theoretical justification - neuroscience motivation is somewhat hand-wavy; no rigorous analysis of why reasoning should remain independent of perception when decoupled
Scalability questions - most evaluations on 4B-8B models; largest model (235B) in appendix; behavior at 70B+ scale unclear
Comparison fairness concerns - 'Thinking with Images' baseline appears to use different model versions (Qwen3-VL 8B vs ChatGPT-3); unclear if training data and setup are identical
Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored - multiple design choices (context window, crop expansion, crop count) with limited sensitivity analysis across task variations
Limited guidance on task-level applicability - unclear when SPARC is beneficial versus harmful; no systematic characterization of task properties determining suitability
